Interface HttpRouteSpec

All Superinterfaces:
ExecutionSpec<HttpRouteSpec>, RouteFilterSpec<HttpRouteSpec>, RouteSpec<HttpRouteSpec>
All Known Subinterfaces:
LocatedHttpRouteSpec<T>
public sealed interface HttpRouteSpec extends RouteSpec<HttpRouteSpec> permits LocatedHttpRouteSpec<T> (not exhaustive)
A pending route to a handler function, declared with a creator of the HttpRouteBuilder, e.g. HttpRouteScope.GET(String): first its settings, then optionally a body stage, then one terminal, which adds the route. 
routes.GET("/items/{id}/name")
    .produces(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_TYPE)
    .handle((request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(items.find(pathVariables.getLong("id")).name()));
routes.POST("/items")
    .consumes(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_TYPE)
    .body(Item.class)
    .handle((request, pathVariables, item) -> HttpResponse.created(items.save(item)));
routes.GET("/old").respond(HttpResponse.permanentRedirect(URI.create("/new")));
  • Settings. The settings it shares with a group, e.g. its media types, executor, annotations and order, are the ones of RouteSpec; a setting of the route overrides the one of its groups. A route on several HTTP methods configures all of them. The filters of the route, see RouteFilterSpec, run after the application's filters and the filters of the groups the route is declared in, closest to the route, and are resolved when the route is built.
  • Body stages. body(Argument), body() and form() declare the body the handler receives: the pending route becomes an HttpBodyRouteSpec, whose terminals take a handler of that body.
  • Terminals. handle(RequestHandler), handleAsync(AsyncRequestHandler) and the respond methods add the route, with the settings given before. A route is ended with exactly one terminal: a second one, or a setting after the terminal, fails with an IllegalStateException. A pending route with no terminal fails the startup, see HttpRouteBuilder.

The route is declared where it is created, in HttpRoutes.routes(HttpRouteBuilder) or in the lambda of its group.

Since:
5.3.0
Author:
Denis Stepanov

  • Method Details

    • responseType

      HttpRouteSpec responseType(Argument<?> responseType)
      Declare the type of the body of the responses of the route, like the return type HttpResponse<R> of a controller method: the message body writer is selected for the declared type, with its type arguments and annotations, instead of the runtime class of the body, e.g. a writer or a JSON view for List<Item> instead of one for ArrayList. The handler still returns an HttpResponse, or a stage of one; a body that is not an instance of the declared type is written as its runtime class, like the body of a controller route. 
      routes.GET("/items")
    .responseType(Argument.listOf(Item.class))
    .handle((request, pathVariables) -> HttpResponse.ok(items.findAll()));

      A response without a body, and a handler that returns no response, are answered like those of a controller route. The route has the declared type for every handler kind, e.g. CompletionStage<HttpResponse<R>> for a handler that completes the response later, and for the features that read the return type of the matched route, see RouteInfo.getResponseBodyType().

      Parameters:
      responseType - The type of the body of the response
      Returns:
      The route
      Since:
      5.3.0

    • body

      <B extends @Nullable Object> HttpBodyRouteSpec<B> body(Argument<B> bodyType)
      The handler of the route receives the body decoded to a type, like a controller method with a @Body argument: the body is read and decoded by the message body readers, with the annotations of the type, e.g. a @JsonView, before the handler runs. The body is required, unless the type is nullable, see HttpRouteBuilder.nullableBody(Argument): then a request without a body is handled with null. The type AsyncRequestBody is the body the handler reads, see body().
      Type Parameters:
      B - The body type
      Parameters:
      bodyType - The body type
      Returns:
      The route, whose terminals take a handler of the body

    • body

      HttpBodyRouteSpec<AsyncRequestBody> body()
      The handler of the route reads the body itself, as an AsyncRequestBody: no binder decodes it, and nothing is read before the handler asks for it. An asynchronous handler, see HttpBodyRouteSpec.handleAsync(AsyncBodyRequestHandler), reads it with methods that complete later or read one element or part at a time, and what its read left open is released when its stage completes. A handler that returns the response, see HttpBodyRouteSpec.handle(BodyRequestHandler), is like a controller method that declares an AsyncRequestBody: what its read left open is released when the request ends.
      Returns:
      The route, whose terminals take a handler of the body
      See Also:
      • AsyncBodyRequestHandler

    • form

      HttpBodyRouteSpec<FormData> form()
      The handler of the route receives the whole submitted form, application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data, as FormData, read before the handler runs. The route consumes both form media types, whatever its groups consume, unless it declares what it consumes itself.
      Returns:
      The route, whose terminals take a handler of the form

      End the route with a handler function, which returns the response: the route runs like a controller method that takes the request and returns a response, and the executor is selected like for a blocking controller method. The handler does not read the body.

    • handleAsync

      void handleAsync(AsyncRequestHandler handler)
      End the route with a handler function that completes the response later. The executor is selected like for a controller method returning a CompletionStage. The handler does not read the body, see AsyncRequestHandler: a handler that does is declared after a body stage, e.g. body().
      Parameters:
      handler - The handler
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the route was already ended

    • respond

      void respond(HttpResponse<?> response)
      End the route with a response computed once, without a handler function: e.g. a constant, a redirect or a static body. 
      routes.GET("/robots.txt").respond(HttpResponse.ok("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /\n").contentType(MediaType.TEXT_PLAIN_TYPE));
routes.GET("/old-docs").respond(HttpResponse.permanentRedirect(URI.create("/docs")));

      The route is an ordinary route: server, group and route filters, conditions, constraints, error routes and CORS apply as for any other route. The response is copied when the route is declared: its status, reason, headers, attributes and body. Each request is answered with a new response built from the copy, so a filter that changes the response of one request does not change the response of the next. The body object itself is shared by the requests: it must not change, e.g. a String or a record.

      The route consumes any content type, as it never reads the body, and produces the content type of the response if it has one, unless the route declares what it consumes or produces itself. It runs no code of the application, so it is answered on the event loop, see ExecutionSpec.nonBlocking(), unless ExecutionSpec.executeOn(String) is set on the route: the executor and the consumed media types of its group do not apply to it. The produced media types of its group apply when the response has no content type.

      Parameters:
      response - The response
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the route was already ended
      Since:
      5.3.0

    • respond

      void respond(Supplier<? extends @Nullable HttpResponse<?>> response)
      End the route with a response the supplier creates for each request, without reading the request, see respond(HttpResponse). 
      routes.GET("/time").respond(() -> HttpResponse.ok(clock.instant().toString()));

      The supplier must return a new response for each request. It is called on the executor of the route, see ExecutionSpec.executeOn(String), or else of its group, and on the event loop when neither has one: then it must not block. A supplier that throws is answered by the error routes, like a handler that throws, and one that returns null like a handler that returns null.

      Parameters:
      response - Creates the response of a request
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the route was already ended
      Since:
      5.3.0

    • respond

      void respond(Function<? super PathVariables, ? extends @Nullable HttpResponse<?>> response)
      End the route with a response the function creates from the path variables of the matched route only, without reading the request, see respond(HttpResponse). 
      routes.GET("/docs/{page}").respond(pathVariables -> HttpResponse.permanentRedirect(URI.create("/guide/" + pathVariables.getString("page"))));

      The function must return a new response for each request. It is called on the executor of the route, see ExecutionSpec.executeOn(String), or else of its group, and on the event loop when neither has one: then it must not block.

      Parameters:
      response - Creates the response of a request from its path variables
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if the route was already ended
